source_text: His compressi erumpunt dicere: (sufficit unicum hoc opus deo nostro, quod hominem liberauit summa et praecipua bonitate sua et omnibus locustis anteponenda\'. o deum maiorem, cuius tam magnum opus non potuit inueniri quam in homine dei minoris! enimuero prius est, ut eum probes esse per quae deum probari oportet, per opera, tunc deinde per beneficia. primo enim quaeritur, an sit, et ita, qualis sit. alterum de operibus, alterum de beneficiis dinoscetur. ceterum non quia liberasse dicitur hominem, ideo esse eum constat, sed si esse constiterit, tunc et liberasse dicetur, ut et an liberauerit constet, quia potuerit et esse et non liberasse. quomodo ergo, quia liberasse dicetur, etiam esse credetur, cum potuerit et esse et non liberasse? . Nunc, in isto articulo ab ignoti dei quaestione deducto si satis constitit tam nihil illum condidisse quam debuisse condidisse, uti cognosceretur ex operibus, quia si fuisset, cognosci debuisset, et utique a primordio rerum, — deum enim non decuisset latuisse — regrediar necesse est ad originem quaestionis dei ignoti, ut ceteros quoque ramulos eius excutiam. primo enim quaeri oportebit, qui postea se protulerit in notitiam cur postea et non a primordio rerum quibus utique necessarius, qua deus, et quidem necessarior quo melior latere non debuit. non enim potest dici non fuisse aut materiam aut causam cognoscendi deum, cum et homo a primordio esset in saeculo, cui nunc subuenit, et malitia creatoris, aduersus quam ut bonus subuenit. igitur aut ignorauit et causam et materiam suae reuelationis necessariae aut dubitanit ++ aut non potuit aut noluit. omnia haec deo indigna, maxime optimo. sed et hunc locum alibi implebimus exprobratione serae reuelationis, sicut nunc sola demonstratione.
pass_a_gloss: These compressed ones burst out to say: it suffices this one work to our God, that He freed man by His highest and principal goodness, which is to be preferred to all locusts. Oh greater God, whose so great work could not be found except in the man of the lesser God! For first, it is necessary to prove Him to be God through those things by which God ought to be proven, through works, then afterwards through benefits. For first, it is asked whether He exists, and thus, what kind He is. One thing will be discerned from works, another from benefits. Moreover, it is not because He is said to have freed man, therefore He is proven to exist, but if it is established that He exists, then He will also be said to have freed, so that it may be established whether He freed, because He was able to exist and not free. How, therefore, because He is said to have freed, is He also believed to exist, when He was able to exist and not free? Now, in this article, having been led away from the question of the unknown God, if it is sufficiently established that He neither created anything nor ought to have created, so that He might be known from works, because if He existed, He ought to have been known, and certainly from the beginning of things, — for it was not fitting for God to have been hidden — it is necessary to return to the origin of the question of the unknown God, so that I may also shake off the other branches of it. For first, it will be necessary to ask, He who later presented Himself to knowledge, why later and not from the beginning of things, for which, as God, He was certainly necessary, and how much more necessary, the better He is, it was not fitting to hide. For it cannot be said that there was not a material or cause for knowing God, since man was from the beginning in the world, to whom He now comes to aid, and the malice of the creator, against which, as good, He comes to aid. Therefore, either He ignored and the cause and material of His necessary revelation, or He doubted, or He was not able, or He did not want. All these things are unworthy of God, especially the best. But we will also fill this place elsewhere with the reproach of the late revelation, just as now with the sole demonstration.

pass_b_english: These critics burst out with a challenge: one act alone is enough for our God — that He freed humanity by His supreme and principal goodness, an act to be preferred above every other. What a greater God, they exclaim, whose greatest work cannot be found anywhere except in the man of a lesser God! But the order of proof is backwards. First you must establish that He is God through the very means by which God ought to be proved — through His works — and only afterward through His benefits. The first question is whether He exists at all, and only then what kind of God He is. Works will decide the one; benefits the other. It does not follow that because He is said to have freed humanity, He therefore exists. Rather, if His existence is first established, then He can be said to have freed humanity — and only then can we verify whether He actually did, since He was able to exist and not free anyone. So how can the mere claim that He freed people make us believe He exists, when He could have existed and done nothing?

Now, since this argument has dragged us away from the question of the unknown God, and it has been sufficiently shown that He neither created anything nor was obliged to create so that He might be known through His works — because if He existed, He ought to have been known, and from the very beginning of things, since it was unfitting for God to remain hidden — we must return to the root of the question about the unknown God, so that I can shake off its other branches as well. First we must ask: why did the One who later revealed Himself do so only later, and not from the beginning of the world, when as God He was certainly necessary — indeed, all the more necessary the better He is — and it was unfitting for Him to stay hidden? It cannot be said that there was no material or cause for knowing God, since humanity existed in the world from the beginning — the very humanity He now comes to aid — and the malice of the Creator existed too, against which He now comes to help as the Good God. Therefore, either He was ignorant of both the cause and the occasion for His necessary revelation, or He doubted, or He was unable, or He was unwilling. Every one of these alternatives is unworthy of God, especially the Best. We will take up this point elsewhere with a reproach against the lateness of His revelation, just as here we press it by demonstration alone.

review.notes: Pass A contains a significant mistranslation of 'locustis' (locusts) which is clearly an OCR error for 'locis' (places) in the source text 'omnibus locustis anteponenda'. While the translator correctly identified the word as 'locusts' in the gloss, the translation 'preferred to all locusts' is nonsensical in context and fails to preserve the sense of the Latin 'omnibus locis' (all places). Pass B correctly interprets the sense as 'above every other [act/place]', but Pass A fails the fidelity requirement by translating the OCR error literally. Additionally, Pass A translates 'tam nihil illum condidisse' as 'He neither created anything nor ought to have created', whereas the Latin 'tam nihil' is a clumsy/corrupt way of saying 'that He had created nothing' or 'that He had not created', and the translation of 'ought to have created' for 'debuisse condidisse' is a reasonable interpretation of the sense, but the 'locusts' error is a definitive failure of sense preservation in Pass A.
uncertainties: 'locustis' is likely an OCR error for 'locis'
reasons: Pass A translates 'omnibus locustis anteponenda' as 'to be preferred to all locusts', which is a literal translation of an OCR error and fails to convey the intended sense of the text (all places/all things).

review.notes: The Latin text is accurately translated in both Pass A and Pass B. The translation preserves the meaning, structure, and theological nuances of the original. All citations are correctly placed and match the content. The title 'Against Marcion's God' appropriately reflects the content of the passage. No errors or omissions are found in the translation or its alignment with the source text.
